title: Communities in the empire
hookLine: Christians and Jews run their own community affairs under Ottoman rule

cards: A wedding in an Ottoman city. The bride and groom are Armenian Christians, and the priest who marries them answers to the Armenian patriarch, not to the local Muslim judge.
Down the street, a Jewish family settles an inheritance before a rabbinic court. Across town, Greek Orthodox children learn their letters in a school run by their own church.
And in the great mosque, Muslims gather for Friday prayer. All of them live under one sultan. Each group handles much of its own life by its own rules.
Today's word names that arrangement: millet.

teach.b: The Qur'an has a word for a religion, a way of faith: milla. It speaks of the milla of Abraham, in Pickthall's translation, "the religion of Abraham, the upright."
In the Ottoman Empire, the word millet came to mean a religious community, with its own leaders and its own law for many of life's matters.
After taking Constantinople, Mehmed saw to it that the Greek Orthodox Church had a patriarch again, and gave him authority over his flock.

teach.h: A PATRIARCH, A RABBI, THEIR OWN COURTS.
teach.b: Armenian Christians had their patriarch. Jews had their rabbis and, in time, a chief rabbi.
Inside each community, marriage, divorce, inheritance, worship, schools and charity were largely run by its own leaders, by its own law. Some readers bring a verse to mind here.
Pickthall renders it: "For each We have appointed a divine law and a traced-out way." Now the honest part, because this was not equality.
Christians and Jews were protected subjects, dhimmis. They paid a special tax, the jizya, and lived under limits that Muslims did not. Muslims held the highest offices.
Some periods and places were generous; others were harsh.
And historians today debate how much of a formal system there was before the empire's last century, or whether the word was used for older, looser arrangements.
Still, for a long time, different peoples of faith lived side by side in the same cities, each keeping its own feasts, its own courts, its own way of marrying and burying.

how: In Turkey today, the Greek Orthodox and Armenian patriarchates and a chief rabbinate still have their seats in Istanbul, a living trace of the Ottoman community arrangements.

games.why: Mehmed saw to it that the Orthodox Church had a patriarch again, who led his community's affairs under the sultan.

practice: Think of a community near you whose ways aren't yours, a church, a synagogue, a mosque, a temple, a gurdwara, and one thing they do that you don't fully understand: a fast, a holiday, a way of mourning.
Be curious about it: what does it protect for them? If you pray, you can ask to see them with respect.

wordCard.voice: Millet. In the Ottoman Empire, a religious community, like the Orthodox, the Armenians or the Jews, running much of its own life under its own leaders. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a religion, a way of faith; in Ottoman Turkish, millet, a religious community.
